newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Labor nominee draws bipartisan support at hearing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Labor nominee draws bipartisan support at hearing.

text.p: Embattled Labour Secretary-designate Alexis Herman sailed through her long-delayed Senate confirmation hearing Tuesday a day after another of President Bill Clinton's nominees quit.

"She's earned her way the hard way, by hard work. And I believe that she will do a good job as secretary of labour," Republican Richard Shelby, from Herman's home state of Alabama, said. Shelby helped derail the nomination of Anthony Lake as director of the Central Intelligence Agency.

Lake withdrew his name on Monday night, saying his confirmation hearing had become a "political circus". He said he could no longer tolerate repeated questions by Republican senators about his integrity, management skills and fitness.
"I look forward to working with you," Senate Labour Committee Chairman Jim Jeffords, a Vermont Republican, told Herman, who has been director of the White House Office of Public Liaison since 1993.
Jeffords said the committee would meet in early April after the congressional Easter recess to send Herman's nomination to the full Senate for approval.

Herman was named by Clinton in December to replace Robert Reich, who resigned at the end of Clinton's first term. Jeffords delayed her hearing for nearly three months while he and other Republicans questioned whether she was improperly involved in campaign activities while at the White House.
They have asked in particular about her role in a White House coffee meeting for several bankers last year which was also attended by Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig, a bank regulator.

Jeffords said Herman had made some mistakes, but added, "Fortunately for all of us, the standard for public office is not perfection. But neither is it sufficient to say 'everybody does it'. They don't."

Almost all the questions at the four-hour hearing were about issues Herman will face as secretary. She said her goals included expanding workers' opportunities for job training and education, improving job safety and equal opportunity and helping welfare recipients find work.

"I want workers to get and keep good jobs. I want working families to enjoy a rising standard of living. And I want workers and their families to have dignity and security throughout their lives," Herman said.

Sen. Edward Kennedy, a Massachusetts Democrat, said Herman's background as a social worker, a businesswoman and as director of the Labour Department's Women's Bureau during President Jimmy Carter's administration made her well-qualified for the post.
"You've just been superb here," Kennedy told Herman at the end of the hearing."

Maine Republican Susan Collins said she was troubled by some of the reports about Herman, but was impressed by her background. Virginia Republican John Warner told Herman, "You have the potential for leadership."
Herman was also endorsed by Jeff Sessions, Alabama's other Republican senator, and all seven House members from Alabama.

Several black leaders attended the hearing to show their support for Herman, who would be the only black woman in Clinton's Cabinet. They included Kweisi Mfume, the head of the National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People, and Transportation Secretary Rodney Slater.
